messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Model
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Eleanor had spent much of her adult life in front of cameras, learning how to stand still, how to turn a shoulder, how to hold her face in a way that suggested ease. At sixty-six, widowed and still occasionally booked for modeling work, she lived in a quiet apartment where the job seemed far removed from the crisis that had divided her life into a before and after. The event itself had happened in a moment that still came to her with terrible clarity: she had been driving in an area she knew well when something went wrong and, in the confusion of the accident, another person was seriously injured. She replayed the scene in fragments, certain that she should have done something more, should have seen it sooner, should have reacted differently. What stayed with her was not only the shock of the impact and the immediate chaos, but the crushing sense that she had been the one who caused the harm, and that another person’s life had been altered because of what she did or did not do in those seconds.

In the weeks that followed, Eleanor found that even when she was home and the doors were locked, her body did not behave as if it had been given permission to stand down. She described herself as unable to relax even in places that were objectively safe, as though some part of her remained braced for the next rupture. She noticed the tension most in her shoulders and jaw, and in the way she sat rigidly at the edge of chairs, always ready to move. Simple moments that once would have felt ordinary became strangely difficult to settle into. She might sit with a cup of tea in the afternoon and realize she had not tasted it at all because her attention kept slipping, snagging on the same images and questions again and again. She reported having difficulty concentrating, especially when trying to read scripts or review work details, and this had become frustrating in a profession that depended on focus and presentation. On set, when she was asked to wait between photos, she could feel her body staying tense under the makeup and clothing, as if it were preparing for danger even though there was none in the studio. The contrast embarrassed her, because she had built a career on composure, and now she found herself fighting to look composed while feeling as though she could not let herself fully soften.

What weighed on her most was the meaning she had attached to the accident. Eleanor was convinced that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, that another woman would have handled the moment with more presence, more judgment, more courage. She spoke about the event with a kind of shame that had settled into her identity, not as something she had done, but as something that marked her permanently. She felt permanently humiliated by what happened, especially because she had always seen herself as careful and competent. In her mind, the accident did not belong to an unfortunate chain of events; it belonged to her character. She returned repeatedly to the same painful thought that she would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. That thought came up when she was alone, when she was lying awake at night, and also in the middle of the day when she would catch herself scanning a room or a street for anything that might go wrong. She knew, rationally, that she was not reliving a headline or a story told by someone else. It was her own life, and that made the humiliation feel private and absolute.

Over time, Eleanor began organizing her days around the wish not to be caught off guard by reminders. Driving had become especially fraught, not because she described a phobia of driving in general, but because being in a car brought her back to the exact kind of moment in which everything had gone wrong without warning. She avoided routes and situations that made her feel trapped in motion, and she arranged her schedule more carefully than she used to, sometimes declining work if it meant too much time on unfamiliar roads. In the modeling world, where people assumed confidence and flexibility, she found it difficult to explain why she needed to keep control over how and where she traveled. The consequences were practical as well as personal: she turned down invitations, was less spontaneous with friends, and sometimes felt pulled away from conversations because she was too busy monitoring how tense her body felt or trying to push away the memory of that injured person and the chaos around them. Her widowhood made the strain more visible at home, where there was no spouse to reassure her or distract her from the silence, and she often felt that her apartment had become a place where the memory could catch her unprotected.

By the time she sought help, Eleanor was tired of living as if she were perpetually one step away from disaster and one step away from disgrace. What brought her in was the wear of carrying the same humiliation and self-reproach day after day, along with the discouraging realization that she could not simply force herself to relax or think clearly again. She hoped therapy might help her make sense of why the accident had come to define her so completely, and she was most afraid that she would remain stuck forever in that same fixed moment, unable to forgive herself and unable to feel at ease in her own life.
